When the Otis family assembled for breakfast the following morning, they talked of the ghost at considerable length. The United States Minister was naturally somewhat vexed that his gift had been refused. ‘I certainly have no desire,’ he remarked, ‘to inflict any personal harm upon the ghost; and, considering how many years he has occupied the house, I must say I regard throwing pillows at him as extremely discourteous’—an entirely reasonable observation which, I regret to relate, made the twins roar with laughter. ‘On the other hand,’ he went on, ‘should he really refuse to employ the Rising Sun Lubricator, we shall be obliged to confiscate his chains. Nobody could possibly sleep with that sort of din outside the bedrooms.’

During the remainder of the week, however, nothing disturbed them. Only the blood-stain, perpetually reappearing on the library floor, attracted notice. This was decidedly singular, since Mr. Otis invariably locked the door at night and the windows remained securely barred. The stain’s chameleon-like colouring also provoked much discussion. On certain mornings it showed a dull red, almost Indian red; then it became vermilion, then a deep purple. Once, when they descended for family prayers, performed according to the plain observances of the Free American Reformed Episcopalian Church, it confronted them in vivid emerald-green. Such kaleidoscopic alterations naturally afforded the household immense amusement, and wagers concerning them were freely laid each evening. Little Virginia alone declined to share the joke. For some reason nobody could explain, the blood-stain always made her very unhappy, and on the morning of its emerald-green appearance she all but wept.

The ghost made his second appearance on Sunday night. Soon after the family had retired, a tremendous crash in the hall startled them. They hurried downstairs and discovered that a great suit of ancient armour had slipped from its support and tumbled onto the stone floor. Meanwhile the Canterville ghost sat in a chair with a high back, rubbing his knees, his face expressive of the keenest suffering. The twins, who had fetched their pea-shooters, instantly fired two pellets at him with that precision obtainable only through prolonged and diligent practice upon a writing-master. At the same moment the United States Minister pointed his revolver at him and, in obedience to Californian manners, commanded him to put up his hands. The ghost sprang to his feet with a furious shriek and streamed through their midst like vapour, putting out Washington Otis’s candle in passing and leaving the entire company in utter darkness.

Lay down your weapons, fellow human beings! Brothers! Repent, and you will find forgiveness, help, and brotherly love waiting for you. We cherish you because you share our fragile human form; every one of you will find a friend and a place to stay among these troops. Must we turn against one another while plague, our common enemy, hangs over us even now, exulting in a slaughter more cruel than its own?”

Both armies stopped. On our side, the soldiers kept a firm grip on their weapons and watched the enemy with hard eyes. The others still held their weapons too, more from fear than any desire to fight. They glanced at one another, each hoping someone would give him an example to follow, but they had no leader. Adrian leaped from his horse and approached a man who had just been killed. “He was a man,” he cried, “and now he is dead. Hurry, bind the wounds of the fallen—let no one die. Let no more souls slip through the merciless wounds you have made to stand before God’s throne and tell of brothers killing brothers. Dress their wounds and return them to their friends. Drive from your hearts the savage fury of tigers; throw down those instruments of hatred and cruelty. In this brief pause in the destruction that awaits us, let each man be a brother, protector, and support to another. Put away those bloodstained weapons, and some of you come quickly to tend these wounds.”

While speaking, he knelt and gathered into his arms a man whose life was pouring in warm blood from his side. The wounded man gasped. Both armies had grown so quiet that everyone could hear his moans; every heart, which moments earlier had been fiercely committed to wholesale killing, now trembled between hope and fear for this single man. Adrian pulled off his military sash and wound it around the injured man, but he was too late. The man gave a deep sigh, his head dropped back, and his limbs went limp. “He is dead!” Adrian said as the body slipped from his arms to the earth. He lowered his head in grief and awe. In the death of this one man, the fate of the whole world seemed to hang. Troops on both sides dropped their weapons. Even the veterans cried, and our men extended their hands to their enemies as love and profound friendship flooded every heart. The opposing forces came together, unarmed and hand in hand, speaking only of how they could help one another. Each side repented: one of its earlier cruelties, the other of its recent violence. United now, they followed the General’s orders to make their way towards London.

“So I shall never speak of that subject, and you may be sure that once we are married, I will never make any unkind complaint about it.”

Now it was essential to stop him.

“You are moving too quickly, sir,” she cried. “You seem to have forgotten that I have not answered you. Please let me do so at once. Thank you for the compliment you have paid me. I understand the honour you offer in asking me to marry you, but I have no choice except to refuse.”

“I am already well aware,” Mr. Collins replied, waving his hand formally, “that young women commonly refuse a man’s first proposal, even when they secretly intend to accept him. Sometimes they refuse him a second or even a third time. Your words therefore do not discourage me at all, and I still hope to marry you before very long.”

“Really, sir,” Elizabeth exclaimed, “that is a remarkable hope after what I have told you. I assure you I am not one of those young women—if such women exist—who would risk their happiness by trusting that a man will ask again. My refusal is entirely sincere. You could not make me happy, and I am certain I am the last woman in the world who could make you happy. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine knew me, I am sure she would think me unsuitable in every way for the position.”

“If I were certain Lady Catherine would think that,” said Mr. Collins, looking very serious—“but I cannot imagine that her Ladyship would disapprove of you. You can be sure that when I next have the honour of visiting her, I shall give the highest praise to your modesty, your careful management of money, and your other pleasing qualities.”

“Really, Mr. Collins, there is no need to praise me at all. You must allow me to make my own decision, and respect me enough to believe what I say. I wish you great happiness and wealth; by refusing to marry you, I am doing everything I can to prevent you from losing either. By making your offer, you have surely done enough to satisfy your concern for my family. You may inherit the Longbourn estate when the time comes without feeling any guilt. So we may regard this matter as finally settled.” As she spoke she stood up, and she would have left the room if Mr. Collins had not spoken again.

“When I next have the honour of raising the subject with you, I hope your answer will be more encouraging than the one you have just given. Still, I am certainly not accusing you of cruelty now, because I know it is a well-established practice among women to reject a man the first time he proposes. Perhaps you have already said as much to encourage my hopes as a truly modest woman could properly say.”
